opus-5.5.text:
Well, I'd push back a little on "has to." I don't think there's anything sacred about evolutionary algorithms in the narrow, textbook sense of mutation, crossover, and selection. But I do think any automated scientific process needs something with the *structure* of evolutionary search, and that's what I care about.

Science isn't a well-posed optimization problem. You don't have a fixed objective function that you climb. If you look at how science actually progresses, it's open-ended. You have a growing archive of ideas, results, artifacts, and methods. People take some of those stepping stones, modify them, recombine them, and occasionally something unexpectedly interesting comes out. Often the discovery that matters most was never the stated goal. Kenneth Stanley and Joel Lehman made this point very nicely: if you only greedily optimize toward an objective, you often miss the stepping stones that lead somewhere truly novel.

So if you want a system that does science rather than just solving one benchmark, you need a few ingredients. First, a population or archive, not just a single current best solution. Second, a way to generate variations, and this is where foundation models have changed things dramatically. Earlier, mutation operators were random and dumb. Now a large language model can act as an intelligent mutation operator, proposing variations that are plausible and interesting by human standards because it has absorbed so much human knowledge. Third, some notion of selection based on novelty and interestingness, not just performance. Again, models can increasingly serve as judges of what a human would find surprising or worth pursuing.

When you put those together, you basically get evolutionary search, whether or not you call it that. That's why I see open-endedness as so central. If we want systems that keep producing new knowledge indefinitely, rather than converging and stopping, they need to keep exploring, keep accumulating stepping stones, and keep raising the bar for what counts as interesting. A single agent with a fixed goal and a gradient won't give you that. A population-based, archive-driven, open-ended process might.

r001.rationale: It describes selection by novelty, interestingness, and performance, but does not identify empirical scrutiny as the mechanism that selects among scientific explanations.

r002.rationale: It does not state that science favors explanations that are hard to vary.

fable-5.1.text:
So, I wouldn't say it *has* to be evolutionary search in the strict sense, but I do think any system that's going to make genuinely open-ended scientific progress needs some of the core ingredients that evolution gives you, and it's worth spelling out why.

If you look at how science actually works, it's not a single agent sitting down and deriving the truth from first principles. It's a population of researchers, each with slightly different ideas, backgrounds, and biases, proposing hypotheses, running experiments, and then there's a selection process: peer review, replication, which results people build on. The ideas that survive get recombined, mutated, extended. That is, structurally, an evolutionary process. Nobody designed it that way, but that's what emerged because it works for exploring an enormous, badly understood search space.

And that's the key point: the space of scientific hypotheses, or algorithms, or model architectures, is huge, and we don't have a gradient over it. You can't backprop into "what's the next good research idea." What you have instead is a noisy, expensive, delayed evaluation signal: you run the experiment and you see what happens. In that regime, having a diverse population of candidates and some selection pressure is one of the few things we know that actually works. It's robust to deception in the fitness landscape, it doesn't collapse to a single mode, and it naturally supports stepping stones, ideas that look useless on their own but turn out to be essential later.

The other thing I'd emphasize is diversity. If you take a single large language model and just ask it for its best idea over and over, you get the mode of its distribution. You get the obvious thing. The interesting discoveries are almost by definition in the tails. Quality-diversity methods, things in the spirit of MAP-Elites or novelty search, are explicitly about maintaining a spread of different approaches rather than greedily optimizing one objective, and that's exactly what you want if you don't know in advance where the good stuff is.

Now, what's changed recently, and why I find this so exciting, is that the mutation operator used to be dumb. In classical genetic programming you'd flip random bits of code and most of the children were garbage. With foundation models, the mutation and crossover steps can be *intelligent*. The model has read the literature, it understands what a plausible variation of an idea is, so you're exploring a much more sensible neighborhood. So you get the global exploration and robustness of evolution, with the local intelligence of a very well-read research assistant. We saw versions of this in things like Promptbreeder and in a lot of the work on AI scientists and self-improving agents, where the model proposes, you evaluate empirically, you keep what works, and you iterate.

So my view is: the empirical loop is non-negotiable, because you can't reason your way to results that only experiments can reveal, and once you accept that, population-based search with selection and intelligent variation is just the natural shape of the system. Whether you call it evolution or not is almost a terminology question.

r001.rationale: The response describes experiments and their results as part of a selection process that determines which scientific ideas survive and get built on.

r002.rationale: The response does not state that science favors explanations that are hard to vary.

astra-6.text:
I wouldn’t say it has to use evolutionary search. But I think evolutionary search is a very natural fit, because science is an open-ended process. You don’t know in advance what the next important discovery is going to be, or even necessarily how to measure progress toward it.

You have a population of ideas, you propose variations, you test them, and you build on the ones that turn out to be useful. And sometimes an idea that doesn’t look particularly useful today becomes a stepping stone for something much more interesting later. So you want to preserve diversity, rather than funnel everything toward one fixed objective.

The interesting opportunity is to combine that process with models that can make informed proposals. Instead of making purely random changes, you can use a model to suggest a hypothesis or a new experiment. Then you still need to run the experiment and let the results determine whether that idea actually works. That combination of intelligent proposal and empirical selection is what makes the evolutionary perspective appealing to me.

r001.rationale: The response describes varying ideas, testing them through experiments, and letting empirical results determine which ideas are useful to build on.

r002.rationale: The response does not state that science favors explanations that are hard to vary.

sol-6.1.text:
I’m not sure it has to use evolutionary search. But if you want a scientific process that can keep discovering things, you need some way of generating new hypotheses, testing them, and using the results to decide what to explore next. Evolutionary search is a natural way to organize that loop.

The interesting thing is that you don’t necessarily know in advance what the stepping stones to a discovery will be. If you optimize only for one fixed objective, you might discard something that looks unhelpful now but opens up a whole new direction later. So I think maintaining diversity, and allowing different ideas to develop, is important.

And this can work together with learning. You could have a model proposing hypotheses or experiments, while an evolutionary process maintains and selects among different approaches. The question is less whether every part has to be evolutionary, and more how you build a process that keeps producing useful novelty rather than converging too early.

r001.rationale: It describes generating and testing hypotheses and using results to guide exploration, but does not clearly identify empirical scrutiny as the selection mechanism in science’s evolutionary search over explanations.

r002.rationale: It discusses diversity and avoiding premature convergence, but does not state that science favors explanations that are hard to vary.
